web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Operating Cycles
question: Where did this business come from, and how has it behaved through its own bad years before you trust the good ones?

epigraph.quote: Stallion started operations in 1992. (Acquired by the company on a Slump Sale basis pursuant to slump sale agreement in the year 2023)
epigraph.author: Stallion India Fluorochemicals, corporate website timeline [13]

web_blocks.html: Start with the company before the numbers got big. Stallion’s own website says it began operations in 1992 and set up its first stand-alone debulking and bottling facility at Panvel, near Mumbai, in 1998. A North India site at Manesar, Gurgaon followed in 2002 [13]. The listed company is younger than that history. It was incorporated as Stallion India Fluorochemicals Private Limited in Mumbai on 5 September 2002 [5]. The website says the 1992 business was acquired by the company on a slump-sale basis in 2023 [13]. A slump sale transfers a running business as a going concern, so the operating record came across with the business rather than starting from zero.

What the company sells is refrigerant gas and the services around it. The RHP says the company has been the Honeywell distributor for HFC refrigerant gases since 2006 [5]. The FY25 annual report’s milestone list records the steps after that: HFO-1234yf supplies to Indian auto makers, a partnership with Daikin for HFC-32 sourcing, isobutane supplies from the Khalapur plant, and a new facility at Ghiloth, Rajasthan [4]. The list is not dated in the extract I read, so treat it as a sequence rather than a timetable.

web_blocks.title: The growth path, in audited numbers

web_blocks.html: Revenue from operations grew from ₹233.24 crore in FY24 to ₹377.45 crore in FY25, a rise of 61.8%, and then to ₹430.68 crore in FY26, up 14.1% [4][1]. Profit moved faster than revenue over the same two years. The table puts the two side by side. The FY24 profit figure comes from the RHP’s restated table, because the FY25 report gives the FY24 revenue comparative but not the FY24 profit line I could check [7].

web_blocks.caption: Revenue and profit after tax, years to 31 March (₹ crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Profit after tax rose from ₹14.79 crore to ₹43.84 crore in two years, about three times the earlier level against revenue that grew about 1.8 times. That is the first thing to test in the margin chapters, not a conclusion yet.

web_blocks.html: The FY26 profit is real in the audited statements. The auditor issued an unmodified opinion on the financial statements and on internal financial controls [3]. Hold that in mind. The same filings show how quickly the picture can change.

The biggest structural change of the last year is not in the income statement. The board authorised a rights issue on 23 January 2026, which the annual report puts at about ₹363.92 crore gross [2]. Net proceeds in the cash flow statement were ₹336.02 crore [23]. Equity capital and reserves together rose from ₹300.84 crore at March 2025 to ₹680.60 crore at March 2026 [1]. Cash and bank balances stood at about ₹433.67 crore at March 2026, against ₹75.01 crore a year earlier [1]. The company now holds a large treasury beside its operating business, and that changes how you should read returns on capital in chapter 6.

The rights issue also changes the arithmetic of the company’s returns. Equity more than doubled in one year, so a profit that looked high on the old base looks lower on the new one. Be careful with the cash figure as well. Cash and bank balances rose by about ₹359 crore in the year, but about ₹205 crore of that went into fixed deposits, which the cash-flow statement shows as an investing outflow [23]. The money is real. It is also a choice about where to park it, and chapter 6 works through the returns on the larger base.

Measured against the closing equity of March 2026, the same ₹43.84 crore of FY26 profit is a return of about 6.4%. Measured against the equity a year earlier, it would have been about 14.6%. The profit did not shrink. The base grew, and the question for chapter 6 is whether the new money earns enough to lift the return back [1].

The RHP gives the cleanest long history. Stallion’s EBITDA margin on the RHP table was 17.71% in FY22, fell to 6.90% in FY23, and recovered to 11.30% in FY24. The PAT margin followed the same path, from 11.33% to 4.31% and then 6.26% [7]. Those are the company’s own trough numbers. They carry more weight than any single good year.

The quarterly series shows the same behaviour at a finer grain [14]. The operating profit margin was 16.89% in the June 2024 quarter, fell to 2.86% in the September 2024 quarter, and was back at 16.81% by December 2024. From then until June 2026 it ran between 11.16% and 18.15%. It fell to 2.20% in the September 2026 quarter [14]. Two of the three weakest quarters in the series are September quarters. The sources I checked do not say whether that is seasonal or something else, so I leave it open.

September 2026 sales were ₹136.03 crore, up 28.87% on a year earlier, yet operating profit was only ₹2.99 crore [14]. Revenue growth and profit can split apart in this business for a simple reason. A refrigerant gas earns a spread over the cost of the imported raw material, and when that spread narrows, extra volume does not rescue the margin. Chapter 3 shows how much of the cost base sits inside that spread.

Two terms in the margin table need a plain reading. EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, so it measures the operating business before financing and accounting charges. Profit after tax is what remains for shareholders after all of them. In FY23 both margins fell together, which shows that the operating squeeze reached the bottom line rather than being absorbed by financing or tax [7].

web_blocks.title: Why one bad year hit so hard

web_blocks.html: A company with several product lines can absorb a bad year in one of them. Stallion in FY22 could not. Refrigerant gases were 95.89% of product sales that year. The share was 83.63% in FY23 and 81.85% in FY24, and it was 87.34% in the six months to September 2024 [25]. Even at its lowest point in the RHP series, the refrigerant line was more than four-fifths of product sales. With so little in other lines, a squeeze on the refrigerant spread went straight through to the profit line. The company has since added helium, specialty gases and the planned R-32 plant. Whether that is enough diversification is the question for chapter 2.

The product share can mislead on its own. The refrigerant share of product sales fell from 95.89% in FY22 to 81.85% in FY24 [25], which looks like diversification. Over the following periods the import cost share rose from 70.23% of revenue in FY23 to 85.00% in the six months to September 2024 [6]. The line got smaller as a share of sales, but the imported input became a larger share of revenue. Adding product lines did not remove exposure to imported raw material.

web_blocks.title: What the history does not show

web_blocks.html: The history here is short. The RHP margin table starts in FY22, the quarterly series starts in June 2024, and the years before the 2023 acquisition are a company timeline rather than audited figures. Before the acquisition the business operated under Stallion Enterprises, and the sources I checked do not give its margins for those years. So the FY22 and FY23 figures are the earliest margins I could verify. A longer cycle may exist, but until a filing shows it, treat any claim about one as unverified.

In the October 2025 analyst call, management said it had promised FY26 turnover of ₹430 crore and profit after tax of ₹40 crore [10]. The audited figures came in at ₹430.68 crore of revenue and ₹43.84 crore of profit after tax [1]. That is a kept promise, and it deserves credit. Chapter 5 takes the later promises one at a time. Most of them have dates that have not yet arrived, so the test is still open.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Revenue up 62% in one year and profit above the promised ₹40 crore in FY26 look like the whole story. The FY23 trough and the two September dips are the other half. Write both down. A history that includes a halved margin tells you what a bad year looks like in this business, and that is more useful than the best year.

Notice the other thing the history shows. The operating business sits inside a company that is younger than its own brand, and its treasury now holds hundreds of crores in cash. That is a different balance sheet from the one that produced the 2023 trough, so the old base rate is a guide rather than a law.

book_paragraphs: Let me walk you through this company the way I would if we were sitting across a table. Before you look at any ratio, look at the history. Stallion’s own timeline says it started operating in 1992, opened a stand-alone debulking and bottling facility at Panvel in 1998, and set up a North India site at Manesar in 2002. The listed company is younger than that. It was incorporated in Mumbai on 5 September 2002, and in 2023 it acquired the older business on a slump-sale basis. So you are not looking at a start-up. You are looking at a distribution and processing business with a long operating record, wrapped inside a company that is still finding its shape.

What it sells is refrigerant gas, mostly, and it has been the Honeywell distributor for hydrofluorocarbon refrigerants since 2006. Over the last few years it has added HFO refrigerants, isobutane supplies, a facility in Ghiloth in Rajasthan, and a helium project at Khalapur. Some of those are small. Some of them are the reason the next three years may look different from the last twenty.

The audited growth is strong. Revenue from operations went from about 233 crore in FY24 to about 377 crore in FY25, and then to about 431 crore in FY26. Profit after tax went from about 15 crore to about 44 crore over the same two years. That is a business whose profit grew faster than its revenue. Good. Now ask the uncomfortable question. Why did the margin fall so far in FY23, and why did it dip again in the September 2024 quarter and in the September 2026 quarter?

The rights issue is the other thing you cannot skip. Late in the year the company raised about 364 crore through a rights issue. Equity went from about 301 crore to about 681 crore. Cash and bank balances ended the year near 434 crore. That money is real, and it lowers the risk of a funding squeeze. It also sits in deposits that earn interest rather than operating returns. Keep that in mind when we get to returns on capital.

Look at the RHP’s margin table, because it is the cleanest long history you have. The EBITDA margin was 17.71 percent in FY22, fell to 6.90 percent in FY23, and came back to 11.30 percent in FY24. The profit margin followed the same shape. Those are the company’s own trough numbers, and I would give them more weight than any single good year. A margin that halves in one year is part of the base rate for this business, not an exception to it.

The quarterly series makes the same point more sharply. The operating margin was about 17 percent in June 2024, dropped below 3 percent in September 2024, and was back near 17 percent by December. It then ran between about 11 and 18 percent until June 2026. In September 2026 it fell to about 2 percent again. Two of the three weakest quarters in the series are September quarters. I do not know yet whether that is seasonal or a sign of something else, and I will not pretend the sources answer it.

Here is one promise you can check. In October 2025 management said it expected FY26 turnover of 430 crore and profit after tax of 40 crore. The audited FY26 numbers came in at 430.68 crore of revenue and 43.84 crore of profit after tax. That is a credit to them, and you should give it. Remember it when you read about the plant timelines later, because a company can keep one promise and still run late on another.

There is one more lesson in the history, and it is about concentration rather than timing. In FY22 refrigerant gases were about 96 percent of product sales. Even at the lowest point the line was more than four-fifths of product sales. When a business is that concentrated, a bad spread in one product is a bad year for the whole company. Stallion did not have a second engine to keep the lights on, and that is why the 2023 trough cut the margin so deeply.

I should also be honest about the limits of the history. The margin table starts in FY22, and the quarterly series starts in mid-2024. Before the company’s 2023 acquisition, the business ran under another name, and I did not find audited margins for those years. So the FY22 and FY23 numbers are the earliest I can verify. If you hear a longer cycle described, ask for the filing that shows it.

Here is the promise again in plain terms. In October 2025 management said FY26 would deliver 430 crore of turnover and 40 crore of profit after tax. The audited accounts show 430.68 crore and 43.84 crore. That is a kept promise. Keep the difference between a kept promise and a sound business in mind as we go.

So where does that leave you? You have a business with a real operating record, a much stronger balance sheet than a year ago, and a margin history that moves a great deal. That history is the lens for the rest of this report. Every later chapter asks the same question. When the spread narrows, does this company have enough scale, product breadth and cash to hold its ground? Keep that question in your pocket as we go.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Revenue up sixty percent in one year and profit above the promised forty crore look like the whole story. The trough in FY23 and the quiet September dips are the other half. Write both down. A history that includes a halved margin tells you what a bad year looks like here, and that is more useful to you than the best year.
